title: Review: Ulysses (Off-Broadway, The Public Theatre) #OffBroadway #TheP...
transcript: I had no idea what was happening at any point in this play. And if you have read Ulysses by James Joyce, which this play is an abridged version of, then you probably know why. As they tell you at the top of the show, this is a famously confusing novel that has been confounding readers since it came out in 1922. And since all of the dialogue in the show is ripped from Joyce's original text, it doesn't do much in terms of helping the audience navigate this story. This show is from Elevator Repair Service, the same team that brought us Gatz, an eight hour long recitation of F. Scott Fitzgerald's novel The Great Gatsby. Ulysses takes a similar approach, although this time the text is abridged, often literally fast forwarding through chunks of the novel and clocking in just under three hours. However, I found Gatz to be a lot more compelling, in part because the story and novel itself are just easier to comprehend, but also because they gave it this meta narrative that ran throughout the piece. That show started with a man who was bored at work during his 9 to 5 and starts reading The Great Gatsby to pass the time. And so, in addition to the themes of The Great Gatsby, it also became this meditation on boredom and monotony and using stories as a means of escape. Ulysses, on the other hand, just starts with actors sitting at a table reading The script. And there is no real meta narrative placed over the text. It's just a far less interesting entry point into the text. And like with Gatz, we do see the story slowly start to consume these actors and this space. And there is a lot of fun to be had in the creative ways in which they are able to stage this text using minimal sets and props. And I found that the second I stopped trying to make sense of the plot or find any kind of through line, I did start to enjoy the show a lot more. You can tell they really wanted to highlight the humor and playfulness in this novel that I think often gets lost by readers who are too concentrated on trying to make sense of what they are reading. So while I was still confused about what was going on at any given moment, I was still generally entertained. If you have never read Ulysses or have struggled with it in the past, don't go into this expecting this to be the thing that makes you finally understand Ulysses. This production is very faithful to the novel, for better and for worse. But if you go in with an open mind and accept that you will not know what's going on, there is still some fun to be had.
